sections.overview: The Mauritian tomb bat is an insect-eating bat of Africa south of the Sahara and of several Indian Ocean islands. It is named after the island of Mauritius, where the first specimen was collected, and is listed as Least Concern.
sections.identification: A small bat with a forearm of 60–66 mm and a weight of about 20–36 g. The back fur is short, sleek and mixed grey and the underside is entirely white. The wings are long, narrow and pale, with shortened tips that help the bat crawl when the wings are folded. Males have a dark spot on the chin.
sections.habitat: It prefers moist, open country and savanna receiving at least about 500 mm of rain a year; in drier areas it is recorded near swamps and rivers. It also occurs in forest and along watercourses. The Mammal Diversity Database gives its range as South Africa to Sudan and Somalia and to Senegal, plus Madagascar and islands such as Mauritius, Réunion and Aldabra.
sections.diet: It feeds on flying insects, with moths as the staple and termites and butterflies as additions. It starts hunting once it is fully dark, spots prey over open ground and never flies above treetop height. It makes dives of up to 10 m, calling faster as it dives, and sometimes darts out of its roost by day to catch passing prey.
sections.behavior: It roosts in the open but out of direct sun, on the outside of walls under eaves or on large tree trunks and palm trunks, choosing spots that allow a clear take-off; it does not use dark hollows or roofs as many bats do. Colonies are small, usually about five and at most about thirty. Roosts are reused year after year. Seasonal movements are suspected but not proven.
sections.reproduction: A single young is born at a time, and the female raises it alone, the young clinging to her belly until it can fly. Gestation is about two months. The timing is not settled: one source gives two birth periods a year, November–December and February–April, while another gives different months.
sections.ecology: By eating large numbers of insects it helps control pests. Snakes and owls prey on it. It can carry parasites of the genus Anchitrema, which may pass between bats sharing the same roost.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Least Concern, as it is widespread across Africa and nearby islands. The sources read name no specific threat. As it depends on exposed roost sites, the loss of suitable walls and trees could matter locally, but this has not been measured.
